subject: CFA: weird value for error covariance in completely standardized solution

messages.author: 25a6c6f4afee9ffa
messages.subject: CFA: weird value for error covariance in completely standardized solution
parts:
Dear all,
 
When I run cfa in lavaan with the following data (from the Lattin, Carroll, and Green, 2003, book), model and call to the cfa-function:
 
# DATA
lower <- '
 1.000
  .638  1.000
  .430   .411  1.000
  .547   .407   .426  1.000
  .776   .600   .355   .516  1.000
  .561   .713   .432   .363   .635  1.000
  .368   .344   .813   .393   .364   .451  1.000
  .490   .370   .418   .764   .531  .366   .361  1.000
  .676   .539   .394   .509   .739  .527   .372   .469  1.000
  .522   .720   .384   .349   .559  .698   .365   .376   .589  1.000
  .339   .323   .791   .351   .335  .366   .783   .340   .365   .367  1.000
  .376   .283   .343   .667   .424  .290   .360   .662   .515   .333   .394  1.000'
 
Store_traits.cov <- getCov(lower, names= c("appear_l","produc_l","prices_l","servic_l","appear_d","produc_d",
                                      "prices_d","servic_d","appear_s","produc_s","prices_s","servic_s"))
#MODEL
cfa.Store_traits2 <- "appear   =~ appear_l + appear_d + appear_s
                     products =~ produc_l + produc_d + produc_s
                     prices   =~ prices_l + prices_d + prices_s
                     service  =~ servic_l + servic_d + servic_s
                     appear_s ~~ servic_s"
 
#CALL TO FUNCTION CFA
fit.cfa.Store_traits2 <- cfa(cfa.Store_traits2, sample.cov=Store_traits.cov, sample.nobs=250, std.lv=TRUE, estimator = "ML")
 
... then I see a weird value for the error covariance between appear_s and servic_s in the completely standardized solution:
 
                   Estimate  Std.err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
  appear_s ~~
    servic_s          0.125    0.030    4.205    0.000    0.125    0.328
 
... that is, I would not expect 0.328, but 0.125, since all variables already have a variance equal to 1 (as I am actually analyzing the correlation matrix).
 
Does anyone have any idea what I am overlooking?
 
Thanks in advance,
Ivo van der Lans

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: CFA: weird value for error covariance in completely standardized solution
parts:
The TOTAL variance of each indicator is 1: the sum of the common variance represented by (squared) factor loadings and the unique variances (i.e., the variances of the disturbance terms for each indicator).  So the unstandardized parameter estimate of the covariance between appear_s ~~ servic_s is not already standardized because the residual variances are not 1, they are some smaller value.  In the completely standardized solution, the residual variance matrix is standardized, so that all residual variances (i.e., variances of disturbance terms) are rescaled to 1, and the corresponding off-diagonal residual covariances are rescaled to correlations.  Basically, this matrix:

messages.author: 25a6c6f4afee9ffa
messages.subject: Re: CFA: weird value for error covariance in completely standardized solution
parts:
Dear Terry,
 Many thanks for your explanation! I now do understand that the estimate of the covariance between two error terms in the completely standardized solution actually gives the correlation between them. For me, that's the most important thing. I am a bit puzzled though about what could be the rationale for not showing the value one (but 1-R^2) for the variance of the error and disturbance terms in the completely standardized solution then. To me it seems as if the covariances between the error terms come from a differently scaled solution than their variances do.
 
Kind regards,
Ivo

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: CFA: weird value for error covariance in completely standardized solution
parts: I am a bit puzzled though about what could be the rationale for not showing the value one (but 1-R^2) for the variance of the error and disturbance terms in the completely standardized solution then. To me it seems as if the covariances between the error terms come from a differently scaled solution than their variances do.

My guess is that the values from the diagonal of the residual correlation matrix are not reported because obviously they will be 1, but that isn't an informative value or one that most researchers would be interested in.  The off-diagonal covariances are interesting in a standardized metric because they are easier to interpret.  But the standardized residual variances are 1 - R^2 (standardized with respect to total observed variance) because that is of interest to researchers.

Terry

parts: Op vrijdag 13 september 2013 20:12:09 UTC+2 schreef Terrence Jorgensen:

My guess is that the values from the diagonal of the residual correlation matrix are not reported because obviously they will be 1, but that isn't an informative value or one that most researchers would be interested in.  The off-diagonal covariances are interesting in a standardized metric because they are easier to interpret.  But the standardized residual variances are 1 - R^2 (standardized with respect to total observed variance) because that is of interest to researchers.

I can see the rationale for not reporting the 1's, as they are 1 by definition. Nevertheless, other variances that are by definition equal to 1, are reported. For instance, common-factor variances in the standardized and completely standardized solution, and variances of the disturbance terms in the unstandardized SEM solutions.
 
I agree that the correlation between unique errors are easy to interpret, still if one would like to report covariances between error terms (with variances 1-R^2) from the completely standardized solution, one now has to reconstruct them oneself, as they are not in the output.
 
I just also noticed that the choice to present the correlation between the error variances in the column for the completely standardized solution is inconsistent with the expected values that come with the modification indices. There, one does get the expected value of the covariance between error terms with variances 1-R^2 in the column for the completely standardized solution, and not the correlation.
 
By the way, I don't think that this is a big issue. Still it could be circumvented by adding an additional column or piece of output that contains the correlations.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: CFA: weird value for error covariance in completely standardized solution
parts:
On 09/16/2013 05:01 PM, ivo.van...@wur.nl wrote:
> .. then I see a weird value for the error covariance between appear_s and servic_s in the completely standardized solution:

>
>
> Estimate Std.err Z-value P(>|z|) Std.lv Std.all
>
> appear_s ~~
> servic_s 0.125 0.030 4.205 0.000 0.125 0.328
>
>
> ... that is, I would not expect 0.328, but 0.125, since all variables already have a variance equal to 1 (as I am actually analyzing the correlation matrix).

This is just a different definition. Interestingly, Mplus 4.1 or older
would have reported 0.125. But newer versions report 0.328.

You can 'switch' between the two versions as follows:

# for the 0.328 version (see element nr 13)
lavaan:::standardize.est.all(fit.cfa.Store_traits2)
[1] 0.8574204 0.9019490 0.8153607 0.8568882 0.8434969 0.8275223 0.9120717
[8] 0.8948297 0.8683147 0.8812643 0.8706250 0.7537703 0.3283569 0.2648303
[15] 0.1864880 0.3351869 0.2657427 0.2885129 0.3152068 0.1681252 0.1992799
[22] 0.2460296 0.2233733 0.2420121 0.4318303 1.0000000 1.0000000 1.0000000
[29] 1.0000000 0.7939579 0.4726158 0.6647278 0.5117308 0.4986659 0.4987489

# for the 0.125 version
lavaan:::standardize.est.all(fit.cfa.Store_traits2, cov.std=FALSE)
[1] 0.8574204 0.9019490 0.8153607 0.8568882 0.8434969 0.8275223 0.9120717
[8] 0.8948297 0.8683147 0.8812643 0.8706250 0.7537703 0.1249241 0.2648303
[15] 0.1864880 0.3351869 0.2657427 0.2885129 0.3152068 0.1681252 0.1992799
[22] 0.2460296 0.2233733 0.2420121 0.4318303 1.0000000 1.0000000 1.0000000
[29] 1.0000000 0.7939579 0.4726158 0.6647278 0.5117308 0.4986659 0.4987489

In the 'old' tradition, off-diagonal residual covariances were computed
by the formula cov(i,j) / sqrt(i.var*j.var) where i.var and j.var are
diagonal elements of OV. In the 'new' tradition, the i.var and j.var
elements are the 'THETA' diagonal elements, as Terry said. The latter
has the advantage that it gives you the correlation between the two
residuals.

I do agree with Ivo that it is a bit illogical that the variances are
not '1', but 1-R^2. We 'assume' this is what the applied users really
want to see ;-)

Yves.
